urdua1.subtitle: {notes} words · both directions, as two cards per word
descSub: The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first; because half the count
The list was drawn by that frequency, and after the first 75 cards the order still follows it (the end of this description says how); because half the count
urdua1.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (Nov 2026). The figures above describe the list as the frequency dealt it. The deck is now {notes} notes, {cards} cards: those 500, and 37 a beginner needs that the list did not hold. Eight everyday formulas that were cards of the phrases deck, the last on the shelf (سلام علیکم, اللہ حافظ, صبح بخیر, شب بخیر, کیا حال ہے, آپ کا نام کیا ہے and two more) and the greeting آداب, which was a card of B1. Zero, thirteen to nineteen and the tens to ninety, which were cards of B1 and A2, so that every number to twenty and every ten to a thousand is here. The twelve months: four were cards of A2 and B1 and eight are English Wiktionary's proper-noun entries, which the list never read. And two sentences of Tatoeba's, جی ہاں and میں بھی ٹھیک ہوں, whose romanisation is joined from Wiktionary's for each of their words. THE ORDER is a teaching order first and frequency after: the first 75 notes are written by hand — the greetings and courtesies, a first exchange, the pronouns and the possessives, the postpositions, fourteen verbs, the question words, zero to ten — and the rest follow by frequency with each closed set together, eleven to a thousand from note 101, the days from note 151 and the months behind them, the colours from note 201. THE PACE: the app gives ten new cards a day, both directions together, which is five words a day: a greeting and thank you on day one, how are you on day four, {days} days for the deck. Taken in the shelf's order — the alphabet, A1, A2, B1, B2, the phrases — A1 runs from day {from} to day {to} and the whole shelf is {shelfNotes} notes, {shelfDays} days, {shelfYears} years; the alphabet can be studied beside A1 instead of before it. WHAT A CARD SHOWS SINCE THIS PASS: on the forms line, where Wiktionary's headword line writes them, the word again with its vowel marks; a possessive's and کا's feminine and plural (میری, میرے; کی, کے); the future on every verb's table; one romanisation scheme throughout; and both readings of a spelling that has two (میں is "I" and, read otherwise, "in"). NOT HERE, because no source this deck is built from defines them: the full greeting السلام علیکم and its answer وعلیکم السلام, the words for please (مہربانی, براہ کرم) and the postposition تک.

urdua2.subtitle: {notes} words · both directions, as two cards per word
urdua2.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (Nov 2026). The figures above describe the list as the frequency dealt it. The deck is now {notes} notes, {cards} cards. Fifteen cards went down to Urdu A1 — thirteen to nineteen, the tens and two months — and a reader who already holds them here keeps them. The compound numbers came here: twenty-one to ninety-nine, each of which has a form of its own in Urdu and has to be learnt, 71 cards that stand together, in order, as the last 71 of the deck. 45 of them were cards of B1 and B2, wherever their frequency fell, and 26 no level held; those are English Wiktionary's entries, built as every other card is. Seventy-two is the other reading of A1's بہتر. THE PACE: the app gives ten new cards a day, both directions together, which is five words a day, {days} days for this deck; taken in the shelf's order it runs from day {from} to day {to}.

urdub2.subtitle: {notes} words · both directions, as two cards per word
urdub2.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (Nov 2026). The figures above describe the list as the frequency dealt it. The deck is now {notes} notes, {cards} cards: 43 compound numbers went down to Urdu A2, where twenty-one to ninety-nine stand together, and a reader who already holds them here keeps them. B2 IS THE TOP OF THIS COLLECTION, AND THERE IS NO C1. Every level is drawn from English Wiktionary's Urdu, about 7,000 words, and after B2 almost nothing it defines is left: a vocabulary of 130 words written for C1 found two entries. A C1 would have been padding, and was not built. The same thinness shows in this deck: 22 of the 1,500 words it was dealt come from the vocabulary written for B2 and the rest are the commonest words left, 528 of them met less than twice in a million words, so it is less a graded upper-intermediate list than the remainder of what the source defines; the numbers, fruits and animals among its abstract nouns are that. THE PACE: the app gives ten new cards a day, both directions together, which is five words a day, {days} days for this deck; taken in the shelf's order it runs from day {from} to day {to}, and the whole shelf is {shelfNotes} notes, {shelfDays} days, {shelfYears} years.

urphrase.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (Nov 2026). The figures above describe the list as it was drawn. The deck is now {notes} expressions — {phrases} everyday phrases, {idioms} idioms and {proverbs} proverbs — because the eight everyday formulas spelled entirely with Urdu A1's words (سلام علیکم, اللہ حافظ, صبح بخیر, شب بخیر, کیا حال ہے, آپ کا نام کیا ہے, کوئی مسئلہ نہیں, میرا ایک سوال ہے) are now cards of Urdu A1, where a beginner meets them in the first weeks and not after B2; a reader who already holds them here keeps them. THE ORDER inside each subdeck is by reading level: first the expressions every word of which is on a card of Urdu A1, then A2, B1 and B2, and last those that use a word no level cards — most of them Arabic and Persian formulas that are said as one piece. So this deck can be begun beside A1 and need not wait for B2. THE PACE: the app gives ten new cards a day, both directions together, which is five words a day, {days} days for this deck.
